query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: If an AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy is surface-engineered under controlled oxygen partial pressure to promote a tightly adherent spinel layer, then it will exhibit higher tribo-corrosion resistance at 800–900 °C compared to conventional Ni-based or CoCr alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy in as-cast or solution-annealed form.
generation.intervention: A specialized surface treatment protocol that induces a stable spinel (or other protective oxide) scale under controlled thermal and chemical conditions (e.g., controlled oxygen partial pressure and temperature).
generation.conditions: Simultaneous mechanically abrasive sliding coupled with corrosive environment at 800–900 °C, reflecting the elevated-temperature tribo-corrosion operational range.
generation.structural_mediator: A dense oxide or spinel layer forming on the alloy surface that suppresses wear and corrosion attack under high-temperature mechanical loads and harsh chemical exposure.
generation.mechanism: Sluggish diffusion in the high-entropy matrix combined with a stable spinel oxide scale on the surface reduce both oxidation and wear rates, resulting in improved tribo-corrosion resistance relative to traditional structural alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Lower mass loss rate and reduced oxide scale spallation during tribological testing in corrosive atmospheres, as compared with commercial Ni-based or CoCr systems under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional polycrystalline Ni-based or CoCr alloys in the same operating environment typically experience accelerated wear and oxidation, leading to higher mass loss and degradation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis may not hold if the alloy composition or oxidation conditions differ significantly, or if mechanical loads exceed the spinel’s stability range, causing scale spallation and failure.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative details on exact oxide composition, film thickness, and tribo-corrosion lifetime remain uncertain without targeted experimentation and verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy coupons and apply controlled oxidation treatments to form stable spinel layers, then perform pin-on-disk wear and electrochemical corrosion tests at 800–900°C against reference Ni-based or CoCr alloys.
measurements: Surface oxide thickness and chemistry via X-ray diffraction or electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If treated AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 samples do not exhibit lower combined wear-and-corrosion rates or fail more rapidly than the reference alloys under the same test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) first appeared in public view in 2010 [ [1] ]. Thereafter, they aroused great concern from researchers at home and abroad. Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The research shows that adding the proper amount of Al, Cr, and Si elements into the refractory high-entropy alloy can form a dense oxidation film on the surface of the alloy in a high-temperature environment, thus improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] ]. Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. decision.trend: Early work on high-entropy alloys for harsh environments has branched into two main directions relevant to the tribo-corrosion challenge: (1) improving high-temperature tribological performance, as in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 (PMC7515071) where spinel formation was shown to enhance wear resistance up to 900 °C; and (2) enhancing high-temperature oxidation and aqueous corrosion resistance, as in WVTaTiCr coatings (PMC10142552) which form protective oxide scales and exhibits good corrosion behavior in 3.5 wt% NaCl. While both approaches yield improved durability, a single system rigorously optimized for combined tribological and corrosive strains at elevated temperatures has not yet been demonstrated.
decision.unsolved: The synergy between wear and corrosion at high temperatures in a single alloy system remains poorly characterized, especially for in situ conditions that involve both mechanical and chemical degradation. Methods to tailor near-surface microstructures so that stable oxide or spinel films protect against both wear and corrosion have not been fully explored yet.
decision.lever: Develop a surface treatment or deposition route for AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5-type alloys to promote tightly adherent oxide or spinel layers under simultaneous mechanical and corrosive stresses at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–900 °C). Key parameters include controlling oxygen partial pressure, temperature, and environment to favor the formation of a durable protective layer that resists both reactive species and abrasive contact.
decision.why: Prior studies indicate that refractory and high-entropy alloys can form stable oxide or spinel scales, conferring excellent high-temperature wear or corrosion resistance separately. A specialized surface engineering approach that selectively induces and stabilizes such phases under combined tribological and corrosive conditions is a natural next step to address the outstanding gap in tribo-corrosion performance at high temperatures.
